segments.text: - What's your sense of the young engineer?

Do they get excited at the
idea that they might have

a chance to work in some of
these more advanced areas
of electronics design and manufacturing?
- Some, yes.
I try to explain to 'em, I said,

what other industry could you
look at the end of your career

and say, I've built product
that's been on satellites,

I've built product that
went onto the Mars rover,

I built product that's
on the Canadian arm?
And I can say that.
That excited me, and it still does

because we're not in a
new generation of product.

So the world of electronics,
it's just gonna take off.
(bright music)
- Hello, everyone,

and welcome to the
"Altium OnTrack Podcast."
I'm your host, Zach Peterson.
Today, we're talking with Paul Cooke,

director of application
engineering at AGC.

Paul is going to be at
the SMTA UHDI symposium
on January 23rd in Peoria, Arizona.
If anyone's gonna be in the Phoenix area,
I highly encourage you to come out
and listen to his very informative talk.
Very happy to have Paul here today.
Paul, thank you so much for joining us.
- Now, that's a funny story.
So originally my biogram was,

I was an electronics engineer
in the Royal Navy in the UK.

And after I did my couple
of tours and my time was up,

at the time my brother was
working for a company called
ISL.
ISL, became the assistant.
So at the time he said,
"Well, why don't you come and work for me,
just part-time process engineering
while you're looking for a job?"
And that was 35 years ago.

So he subsequently moved
outta the industry,

still calls me up and say,
"How's that part-time job going?"
And I said, "Yep, I'm still doing it
and I'm still looking for that other job."
So I'm getting long in the tooth,

I don't think the other job's
coming anytime soon, so.
So that's how I get into it.

Background, primarily
the first 10, 15 years,

it was application engineering,
process engineering, NPI.
It's funny how things come full circle.

So way back then, we were doing
first generation microvia.

We were doing, and all the
challenges that involved.
I would metalize these really small holes
and the whole industry was changing.

SMTA, our surface mining
technology was coming along.

And everything was a challenge,
but we get through it.
And then every 20 years,
a whole new raft of challenges come along.
I've also been director of quality,
director of process engineering,
so a pretty extensive background.

In the last five years I've
really been involved mostly,

especially with AGC, in
new material development.
And a lot of that we develop
some of our older resin systems.
And I'll talk later about,

but we're developing them
for now older HDI industry.
- So, could you also, briefly,

before telling us about
some of those new materials,
just tell us about AGC?
- So AGC is about a $15 billion company.

They're actually the
largest glass manufacturer
in the world.

So they make glass for
automotive, for touchscreens,
for phones.

But they don't actually make
any glass for our industry,
which is funny, so.
We're, our CCL,

part of the business I work
for is one of 200 companies,
and around 55,000 employees.
So we're a global company.

Our R&D lab in Tokyo has
around 2000 engineers working

on new products, developments
and different systems as well.
So a fairly large multinational company.

- As the electronics industry
has gone on over the past 20
to 30 years or so,

of course miniaturization
has been a big part of that.

And I think that's a good
segue into the UHDI symposium,
where you are going to be speaking.

And of course, working at
a materials manufacturer,

I'm sure you have some
insight into the materials
that are being developed to support
some of these more advanced designs.

What can you tell us about
some of those material systems
that are available for UHDI,

or what is the ideal
material system for UHDI PCB?

- Part of the challenge
is material availability.

The challenge for us
as a material supplier

is each OEM wants a material
that meets every need.
He wants the best mechanical material,
the best electrical material,
unfortunately kind of everything.

So we've spent the last 15
years in very specialized
or fastRise products, developing them for,

we started off developing
'em in early 2000s
for the military.
And one of the first products,
I'll actually talk about that next week,
is a material called EZpure.
'Cause one of the challenges I always had
in fabrication using teflons was,

if you were trying to
bond teflon to teflon,

we use a process called fusion
bonding, or you're using LCP.

So Tom McCarthy developed a
fabricator friendly material

to actually laminate
teflon materials together,

and is still one of the lowest
lost resin systems available
out there.
Next week, I'll actually demonstrate
how that resin system got developed
into a whole bunch of variations.
In the last five years,

I've been working on a
variant called fastRise TC,
the latest ones HF.
And the fastRise TC

is what we call our
indestructible material.
I'll explain next week that we were able
to take that material through 200 reflows

in a five stack microvia and
couldn't break the microvias.
It's a non reinforced,

so I'm part of a front
that I'm classifying
as the non reinforced revolution.

Because really, to go
forward we have to get glass
out of some of this product.

Secondly, we had to
develop products available
and made here in North America.

'Cause a lot of materials
that are available in Asia,

but they're very difficult
for North American fabricators
to basically get their hands on.

We also wanna develop materials
that were process friendly.

So they're much easier for
fabricators here to use.
They don't need to freeze them
and they can use 'em right out of,
like a standard preprint.

And we're now working
on the next generation
of these products,

which are basically going to
be the performance of PTFE,

but not being Teflon components
to the materials themselves.
So they're basically gonna be like a PPO,

PPE type resin system,
but DKs of around 2.2.
So that's in current development,
but we have materials available out there
that are indestructible.

We can make them as thin
as one mil, 1.2 mils thick.

But obviously soon as we
have it, large OEM comes,

"Well, I want 20 microns,
I want this, this, this."
So we have variants

that are just basically getting
developed for specific OEMs
for their need, so.

But yeah, materials is
gonna be the big challenge
for ultra HDI.

- First thing, you mentioned
that we wanna get glass
out of the materials that we're using
for some of these more advanced designs.

And I think most
designers who are familiar

with high speed design will
of course look at the glass
and they'll say, "Oh, fiber weave effect."

But with spread glass
in a lot of laminates,

the spread glass helps reduce
that quite significantly.

So that for a lot of
applications, maybe not all,
but for quite a lot of applications,
the skew gets reduced naturally.
And so you don't have to,

you're not required to do
the zigzag kind of routing
that you sometimes see in some PCBs.

But are there other
reasons to remove the glass
from these products?
- So back before your day probably,

we used to have to rotate
designs 15 degrees on the panel
to try and alleviate scoop.
The days before spread glass.

The challenge with spread
glass is it's very difficult.

If you imagine how they
make the spread glass,

we basically coat the material
and there's resin both sides.

And the resin might be
slightly different one side
to the other.
So the problem is these newer,
higher performing electrically materials,

there's what we would call
a stiffer resin system.
So it's harder for the fabricator
to move that through a spread glass.

So normally what you would
do is when you're designing
a specific dielectric thickness,

you'd say, okay, I'll just
use two plys of that preprint.
But if that's against the heavier copper,

it's now difficult to
move the resin on ply two

down through the second
ply to basically do infill.

So fabricators are having
difficulty with heavier copper
on some of these stiffer resin systems.
So two things we've developed
is really high flow resin systems.

So the one I'm talking about
is gonna been around a 70
to 75% flow content.

Secondly, if we remove
glass, you've removed skew.
If you remove the skew effect

'cause you're working
with a pure resin system,
it's completely homogenous.

And so we have a couple
of different variants
where we can basically predict
the thickness of the material.

Secondly, I'll talk about
this next week, is flatness.
So one of the challenges we have today,

I mean if you talk to Intel,
Intel's making packages
that are four and a half inches in size,
with nine to 12,000 IOs.
The problem they'll have is the flatness

of that package trying
to collapse it in one.
So they're now asking fabricators

if they can produce flatness
of less than a hundred microns
across that four and a half inch package.
And you know when you design a board

just with a telegraphing
and copper distribution,

that you're going to get
variance across the board.
So I've talked to some fabricators,

and I've actually showed
them that using just one ply
of these non reinforced materials
actually got self leveling material,
which gives you that flatness.

So one fabricator took
that surface flatness

from about 160 microns across
four inches down to 60.

So, and if you imagine as
miniaturization gets smaller

and smaller, flatness is
gonna be key to that as well.
So it's, yeah,

there's challenges people
haven't even thought about.
Assembly is a big one, so yeah.

- Yeah, and I think
that's part of the purpose
of the UHDI symposium,

is to kind of see the
convergence of all those issues,
starting from the materials
and then working its way into assembly.
- So with glass,

there's a limit to how
thin we can actually go.
- [Zach] Sure.
- We've actually recently developed

a one and a half mil thick
glass reinforced material.
But the problem is,

for me to get higher
electrical performance,
I need to increase the resin content.

If I increase the resin content,
I increase the thickness.
So there's a limit to how thin.

I mean, we're playing
around with 10, 17 glasses,
trying to get to one mil.
But the challenge is,
is making laminates that thin with glass,

it's high risk for calf and a
whole bunch of other issues.
Whereas with an unreinforced resin system,
I can easily get to one mil or 1.2 mils
in thickness consistently
- That makes a lot of sense.
But with the elimination of glass,

I think someone would assume
that the glassless material
is going to have lower rigidity.

It's going to be basically
like a wet noodle.

And that's a term I've heard
used by applications engineers
at other companies.
Are the materials that you're working on,

do they maintain their
rigidity even when you get down
to these one mill thicknesses?
- No, they're flexible.

- They're very flexible,
okay, unfortunately.
- But if you look at substrate buildup,
there's always a glass core.

So provided there's a glass
rigid core in the center,

then you can do a buildup
technology from that.

So yeah, you're gonna have to
have some rigidized material

in the center of the stack or
somewhere in the stack, so.
- So coreless packages are out?
- Yeah, it's, well we're playing around.
We have another division

that actually lives in
the substrate world,

so they're developing
different types of substrate
for different challenges.
The second reason we developed

some of these materials
was they're very low CTE.

So for instance, our fastRise
TC is a CT of around 22 PPMs,
very close to copper.

Which is really why we
were able to eliminate

that Z expansion and
basically match the copper.

And you don't get this, I'll
actually demonstrate next week,
well I'll talk about it next week,
but you don't get this massive Z expansion
to put stress on microvias.

And the problem is, at
the older HDI world,
we're not talking five mil microvias
which North America is used to building,

we're talking about
threes and twos and ones.

So unless you can do that with
a material with a low CTE,
you would really run into a whole bunch

of assembly issues building
these small microvia structures.
We did some testing with one fabricator,

and they were doing three
mill stacked microvias,

and they were able to do internal
testing up to 300 cycles.
The next best material was 30.
So it's a magnitude batter in performance.

So there's a whole, with
lower X, Y and Z CTE,
you're helping the fabricator get a shot
at building some of this product.

- So some of these materials
that you're working on,
how do they compare to the products
that you are competitors maybe working on
to try and also get ultra HDI?

Or are the goals pretty
consistent across companies

that work in the materials
side of the industry?

- Well, if you talk to
anybody here in North America

that's doing or attempting
to do any buildup technology,
it's material availability as well.

So the guys, your Modo or
some of the other materials
that are available out there,

they're readily available
and used in volume in Asia.
So the volume that's gonna be start off
here in North America is gonna be low,

so material availability is
gonna be maybe a challenge.

I don't know, 'cause I dunno
what the supply chain is like
with some of our competitors.
But from what I hear,
just handling and processing and getting

some of these materials
can be difficult as well.
The other challenge we're seeing is,

our large AI friends
are basically consuming
a whole chunk of the world's materials.
We're starting to see shortages
in certain high performance glass.
So we are actually looking

at how to put our high
performing resin system

just in standard e-glass so
that that's readily available

with decent performance
for designers to use.

But any our glass, they're
now talking about quartz,
but it's just the availability
of some of these glass materials, so.

They're just being consumed
by the larger OEMs.

- This is interesting
what you're bringing up
around availability,

because the conventional
narrative about availability

of electronic components
over the past few years has,
of course, all focused on semiconductors.

And then here in the US,
you have the CHIPS Act,

and of course that drives
this huge amount of investment
in semiconductor fabrication capacity.
And a lot of that was public money,

but an even larger share
of it was private money
by these companies directly.
And the numbers are a significant fraction

of a trillion dollars, so
it's huge amounts of money.

Compare that to the
investment in the supply chain
for PCBs and packages.

It seems like we've had
pretty much nothing,
unless it's part of an NDAA.
It sounds like companies in the industry
are recognizing this.

Do you think that this
might spur off a round

of private investment, or
are the margins just too low

and they're too many
other good alternatives?
- I mean, if you're,

I know most of the fabricators
that have received funding,

it's well south of 200
million, well, well south.
So it's a fraction.
And as we try to explain to US government
and folks out there, chips don't float,
they have to go somewhere.
Everything needs printed circuit ports.
And every week, (clears throat) excuse me.
Every week, every month,

I hear about more and more board
shops that are just running
into financial problems.

And the challenge we have is
there's been no real investment
in PCB manufacturing here for 20 years,
unless they're the large manufacturers.
So a lot investments went into Asia,
and that's why they're probably 15,
20 years ahead of us in technology.
So we're playing catch up.
We're playing catch up with no funding.
Technology needs new equipment.

Ultra HDI is a whole different
mindset for equipment,
processing, et cetera as well.

I mean, TTM setting up a
new facility up in Syracuse,

and that's a fairly major
investment for them.

And that's gonna be a HDI,
ultra HDI type facility, so.

But they're targeted in a
certain sector of the industry.
So, I think it's a challenge.

I think we really need
government to step up
and fund our industry.
The whole supply chain.

Even we are struggling
just with price increases
with glass, with copper.

To manufacture product
here in North America,
it becomes less competitive compared
to bringing in materials from Asia.

- I mean, with all the investment
in semiconductors, right?

those companies and the
people who work in them,
I mean, they're not naive.
They know that they're,

that the components
they're producing, right?
the semiconductors they're producing,

they have to be packaged
in something, right?
So they know they need substrates.
Why haven't they done any work

to try and invest in this area
with materials and packaging
and ultra HDI or any of this?

Is it the same issue, it's
just too low margin or?
- It's because they can get it packaged
at lower cost elsewhere in the world.
It really is.
So I mean, the US only produces around,

they produce around 12%
of the world's chips,

but that still has to go
to Asia to get packaged
then shipped back.

So even if the US was making
60 or 80% of their chips,

they would have to be sent
elsewhere to get packaged
and then brought back in.
So it doesn't really help the supply chain
just to have chip manufacturing.
From a security perspective, maybe,
but from the whole supply chain, no.

There's so much more
involved in a supply chain.
And that can't be done overnight.

You need to start looking
at every aspect of it.
From the resin systems we produce,

all the way through to making
materials, to making PCBs,
before you even get to semiconductors.
So it's, yeah,

it's a big business that
migrated over a long time,

and it's gonna take a
long time to bring back.
So it's gonna be interesting.
- Yeah, yeah.
And with all that business going overseas,

I'm sure it really has
helped to grow the capacity

and availability of
those materials overseas,
like you mentioned.

And it's kind of a chicken
and egg problem, right?
The materials aren't available here

because the business isn't here,
but the business isn't here

because the materials
aren't available here.
- Yeah, and the second challenge is,
it's very difficult for fabricators here,
especially in PCBs,

because they're doing
high mix, low volume.

So if I take you to shop,
a large shop in Asia,

they'll have dedicated lines
for certain technology,
that doesn't change.

And then of another process
line for a different technology.

The challenge with a
North American fabricator,
he could be doing RF product one minute,
he could be doing HDI the next minute.
So it is very difficult to dial in

and get really efficient at
any one type of technology.
So unless there's major investment
that he can invest in a lot of equipment,
and that's all cost, so.
And then the other challenge is
I can buy the same equipment in Asia

for a third of the price I
can buy in North America.
So he's in sort of catch 22.
And it's really hard

for him to compete against
product being brought
in from Asia.
It really starts with the tier one OEMs.
They need to basically say we need
North American manufacturing.

I mean, Tesla have their own
facility now down in Texas,
and that's growing, so that's good.

But we need other large tier
one OEMs to do the same thing.

We need the US military
to help out as well, so.

'Cause they're the guys
with all the dollars
that can help our industry.
- Sure, that makes sense.

I mean, to an extent it
appears that they are kind

of drivers of this, the
US military that is.
Not just because,

of course they have the
unlimited checkbook,

but also because they tend to
work on, or not all the time,
but they tend to work on some technologies
that kind of require
some of these more advanced capabilities.

And that of course then drives
those dollars being spent
here locally in the US
- There's no easy solution, so.
- [Zach] For sure, for sure.
- Unfortunately, so.
I mean, I'd say the US military

is starting to take it
much more seriously.
So we do deal with a lot

of the large tier one
military customers, and yeah,

they're starting to look at
adopting a lot of our materials
or they're gonna investing,

partnering with some of
the higher end PCB shops
here in North America as well.
So we do see that happening.
Not at the speed we want it to happen,

but it is certainly
happening, so which is good.

It really is something we've
needed for a long time.
- So the other side of that,

and I think this is a
good segue back into SMTA
and the UHDI symposium.

I think the other side of
that coin with reshoring

of manufacturing, whether
it's here or Europe,
is workforce development.

Because even if you had all
this manufacturing capacity
in terms of facilities and factories
and raw material availability,

it kind of doesn't matter
if you don't have people

who are knowledgeable
about these processes

and about the materials
and about the designs

to be able to step up and
run all of this stuff.

So do you see that as
a really critical role
for organizations like SMTA,

and then maybe to a
secondary extent, IPC, PCEA,
some of these other organizations?
- So unfortunately,

about 60 to 65% of the
brand trust is my age, so.
(Zach laughs)
And we, I mean certainly I do,

I try and do as many
training session, boot camps,
get out to see,

try and get that knowledge
into young engineers.
Because when my generation retire,

that's a lot of knowledge
that's been lost, so.
And we've had a lot of tried and tested,
especially in process and fabrication,
what works, what doesn't work,
and basically how to go about it.
So we have a problem recruiting engineers
for our industry for sure.
It's not a sexy industry.
People see it as a dying industry,
so it's difficult for, for instance,

board shops to try and
affect young talent.

Not even affect it, it's
trying to keep that talent.
So a lot of them can get a young engineer,

but they can only hold onto
'em for two or three years.

So you invest that time and
effort into a young engineer,
and then he leaves.

So yeah, it's becoming a
challenge for board shops
to attract the right people.
So you're absolutely right.

And there's not a university
teaching PCB fabrication
and design.
And hopefully there should be.

But I'm talking to some
of the universities

to maybe set up seminars and
try and get them interested
in our industry.
- Yeah, I hear a lot of folks who I,
are much more experienced than myself,

meaning they've been around
in the industry longer,
kind of lament this.

And in fact, I was just
talking to Tara Dunn,
and she told me she remembers a time

when there were something
like over 2000 board shops
in the United States.

And about 90% of that, I
think has dwindled down
and gone overseas at this point.
- That's exactly right.

There was 2200 board
shops here I remember,
and it's now down to about 140.

And of that 140, probably 67
to 70 are under 5 million.

So they really are not high
technology board shops,
so they're just treading water really.
So that's part of the problem too, so.
- It is unfortunate for sure.

Now, you said you do a lot
of boot camps and seminars
and conference talks and things like this.
I'm sure you have a chance to meet

some of the younger
talent that's out there.
And you're speaking into an area

that is more at the
advanced level, I would say,

of what we would consider
electronics design.
What's your sense of the young engineer?

Do they get excited at the
idea that they might have

a chance to work in some of
these more advanced areas
of electronics design and manufacturing?
- Some, yes.
I try to explain to 'em, I said,

what other industry could you
look at the end of your career

and say, I've built product
that's went on to satellites,

I've built product that
went onto the Mars rover,

I built product that's
on the Canadian arm?
And I can say that.
That excited me, and it still does

because we're not a new
generation of product.

So the world of electronics,
it's just gonna take off.

And you're in a world where
everywhere you look around you,
you're involved in.

From this conversation,
it's all about electronics,
everything's about electronics.

The car you're driving, the
phone you're picking up.
There's no one industry in the world
where you can basically say,

look around you, I'm involved
in everything all around me.

So get excited about it, and
get into it, and absorb it,
and get as much information.

It's probably one of the
most diverse technologies
in the world as well, so.
And you can go from a designer,
to process engineer and applicate.

There's just so many avenues
you can actually take
as a young engineer, so.
Unfortunately, a lot of the engineers
I would hire would say,

"Well, there's about three
years of your college
that you learned that you need to forget.

We're gonna retrain you
on what you actually need
Quality, and process control and SPC."

But yeah, there's so many
disciplines in this industry

that you could adopt or
change over time, so.
And find something you like to do, so.

- I feel that software kind
of gobbled up a generation
of engineers who probably had the talent

to go and do something in
the electronics industry.
But you look at,

I think popular conception
of software starting

when I was a kid and then
kind of persisting until now.
And then the way that,

I think the media
discusses technology, they,
whenever they use the word technology,
they're always referring to software.

They're never referring to
all the hardware that you need
to run the software in the first place.

I think it's really done a
disservice to our industry
for all of that to happen.
The universities,

I think have kind of
perpetuated that as well.

Because now, all of the electrical
engineering departments,

they kind of cross list
into computer science.
And I think it's been a way

for them to really keep
the department alive.

- Yeah, I mean, I used to go
up to a few colleges and teach.

And I would ask the class,
what do you want to be?
Most of the hands went up, design,
or they wanted a desk based job, so.
And I just thought,

why are you not getting
into manufacturing?

Because it's such an
open universe out there.
Get out there.
And if you wanna do software,
you can do it within our industry as well.
So everything from SMT or assembly,
all the way through to CAM engineering.

There's a whole bunch
of software engineering
you can get involved in, so.

But eh, manufacturing's always
looked as a dirty process.
That's the only thing, so.
- [Zach] Sure.
- It's not a sexy process like...
And the scary thing is,
I go out and do a lot of these seminars
and I talk to designers and I say,

well, how many of you
been in a board shop?
So probably only 20% of designers have
ever been in a board shop.
It's just, it boggles my mind.
And I was at a customer two weeks ago,

and three years ago they
weren't doing any microvia work.
And he says, "Who can build this?
It's a 26 layer seven stack microvia."
And I went, "Well, who designed this?"
He said, "Oh, we designed it ourselves."
I said, "But you aren't doing microvias."

There really should be
courses and more classes
for designers to learn about PCP.

Part of your job as a
PCP designer should be

you have to spend six more
months in a board shop
just to see how it's built,
and then you'll start to understand.

So I'm actually doing a
bootcamp, a design con,

and it's a whole day, of how
PCB design affects fabrication.
And I explained to them about drill sizes,

and it just blows their mind
that, "Wow, we didn't realize."
I said, yeah, 10 mil via to you looks
